content: Oregon-grape, scientifically known as Mahonia aquifolium and belonging to the family Berberidaceae, is an evergreen shrub closely related to the barberry. Some taxonomists classify Mahonia within the barberry genus, Berberis. Despite its name, the Oregon-grape is not botanically related to true grapes. Its name derives from the appearance of its purple berry clusters, which resemble grapes in color and have a slightly dusted surface. This plant is sometimes referred to as Tall Oregon-grape to differentiate it from other species such as Creeping Oregon-grape (M. repens) and Cascade or Dwarf Oregon-grape (M. nervosa). The name is often written without a hyphen as Oregon grape, though this can lead to confusion with actual grape species. Occasionally, it is also seen in print as Oregongrape. Oregon-grape typically grows to a height of 1 to 5 meters. Its leaves are leathery and resemble those of holly, while its stems and twigs have a thickened, corky texture. The plant produces attractive yellow flowers in late spring. It is commonly used in landscaping, much like barberry, as it is well-suited for low-maintenance plantings and loose hedges. Oregon-grape is drought-resistant, tolerates poor soil conditions, and does not produce excessive leaf litter. Its berries are known to attract birds. The small, purplish-black fruits of the Oregon-grape are quite tart and contain large seeds. Locally, they are sometimes mixed with salal berries to make jelly. However, the fruit is bitter and generally requires sweetening before consumption. Due to the holly-like, wilt-resistant nature of its leaves, the foliage is occasionally used by florists as greenery, and a small industry for this purpose exists in the Pacific Northwest. The inner bark of the larger stems and roots yields a yellow dye. Oregon-grape is native to the west coast of North America, ranging from British Columbia to northern California. It is commonly found in the understory of Douglas-fir forests and in brushlands. It is also the state flower of Oregon. However, in some regions outside its native range, Oregon-grape has been classified as an invasive exotic species, capable of displacing native vegetation. Medicinal Use Oregon-grape has been used medicinally by herbalists. Recent research has identified that Mahonia aquifolium contains a specific multidrug resistance pump inhibitor (MDR inhibitor) called 5'-methoxyhydnocarpin (5'-MHC). This compound has been shown to reduce bacterial resistance to antibiotics and antibacterial agents. The root of the Oregon-grape is frequently used as a medicinal alternative to the threatened plant goldenseal. Both plants contain the alkaloid berberine, which is recognized for its anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties and is used in the treatment of infections. Berberine and other alkaloids found in Oregon-grape root have demonstrated the ability to kill a wide range of microbes and have been effective in accelerating recovery from conditions such as giardiasis, candidiasis, viral diarrhea, and cholera. Additionally, Mahonia aquifolium has been shown to be effective in treating inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema and psoriasis. The root of the Oregon-grape also exhibits anticancer properties, which are currently being studied further by researchers. Other potential medicinal actions of the plant include its use as an alternative, diuretic, laxative, and tonic. Health Warning Due to the potential toxicity or adverse effects of berberine, it is essential to consult a reputable herbalist regarding appropriate dosages and treatments. The use of berberine is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
